label: Review of Topology
notes: Appendix A spans printed pages 596 through 616 and supplies the point-set vocabulary every later chapter assumes. We treat it as the contract behind the manifold definition: open sets are the primitive data, and Hausdorff plus second-countable are exactly the two topological hypotheses we will keep demanding.

label: Open Sets and Derived Operations
notes: Stress that a topology is not a distance but a declared family of open sets closed under arbitrary unions and finite intersections. Interior, closure, exterior, and boundary are all derived from that family. The finite non-Hausdorff example in the notebook makes every one of these operations checkable by hand.

label: Bases and Generating a Topology
notes: A basis lets us specify a topology economically: name a few open sets and let unions do the rest. Second countability, one of the manifold axioms, is precisely the demand that some basis be countable. Remind students that metric balls form the standard basis of Euclidean space.

label: Continuity by Preimages
notes: This is the conceptual pivot of the appendix. Continuity is a backward test: preimages of open sets are open. The Sierpinski example shows a map into two points is continuous exactly when the level set of the open point is open, which is why inverse images, not formulas, are the native language here.

label: Homeomorphisms
notes: A homeomorphism is a continuous bijection whose inverse is also continuous; only then are the two spaces topologically identical. Warn loudly that a continuous bijection need not be a homeomorphism. The half-open interval wrapping onto the circle is the canonical counterexample, and it returns when we build quotient manifolds.

label: Subspace, Product, Quotient
notes: Each construction redefines the continuity test. Subspace topology tests after the inclusion, product topology tests every coordinate projection, and quotient topology tests after the projection. Emphasize the quotient subtlety: a set downstairs is open exactly when its saturated preimage is open, so open is not enough unless it is saturated.

label: Hausdorff and Second-Countable
notes: These are the two topological conditions baked into the definition of a smooth manifold. Hausdorff separates distinct points by disjoint open sets, killing pathologies like limits that are not unique. Second countability gives a countable basis, enabling partitions of unity and compact exhaustions. Both fail in the deliberately broken finite models.

label: Compactness
notes: Compactness is the finite-certificate principle: every open cover admits a finite subcover. Walk through the picture of an arbitrary cover collapsing to finitely many sets. Note the two stability facts we reuse constantly: continuous images of compact sets are compact, and finite products of compact spaces are compact by the tube lemma.

label: Connected and Path-Connected
notes: Connectedness forbids splitting the space into two disjoint nonempty open sets; path-connectedness asks for actual paths. Path-connected implies connected, but not conversely. Local path-connectedness is the bridge: there components are open and equal the path components, which is exactly the regime manifolds live in.

label: Convergence and Countability
notes: Sequences only fully characterize topology when countability is present. In the trivial topology a constant sequence converges to every point; in a Hausdorff space limits are unique. First and second countability are what let sequential arguments replace net or filter arguments, which is why we lean on them throughout the manifold theory.

label: Fundamental Group and Coverings
notes: Homotopy turns loops into algebra. The fundamental group records path-homotopy classes of loops at a basepoint. The universal cover of the circle, the exponential map from the real line, makes winding number an integer lift. The degree-n cover sends a loop to a closed lift exactly when its winding is a multiple of n.

label: Synthesis for Manifolds
notes: Pull the threads together into a diagnostic checklist for any later construction: name the open sets or the defining map, test continuity by preimages, check saturation for quotients, verify Hausdorff and second-countable, and ask which invariant survives. This is the lens through which every manifold-building step in the book should be read.
